summary: A 1970 note by M. Elie with comments on memory allocation control commands named CEASE, ALL, GVB, RET and RFNM. These are commands relating to managing buffer space between hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: This note comments on commands that let a computer tell another how much it can accept.

questions: how should flow control and error recovery work
subtitle: Simplifying the buffer allocation scheme with better acknowledgments.

tldr.problem: The current buffer allocation mechanism uses two parallel control schemes (CEASE, ALL, GVB, RET) that are complicated. RFNM is sent before the host fully receives the message, creating synchronization issues and preventing end-to-end error detection.
tldr.mechanism: Replace the complex scheme with a simpler point-to-point transmission procedure. The receiving host sends ACK (CONTINUE) or ACK (CEASE) based on whether buffer space is available, and NAK (REPEAT) if an error is detected. The IMP no longer needs to manage allocation; it is purely a flow-control signal.
tldr.outcome: This simplifies both the protocol and the memory allocation, reducing control message overhead and enabling end-to-end error detection with checksums. The receiving process does not need to understand allocation; it sees only a varying transmission speed.

today: RFC 68 is Unknown status. The proposal for ACK/NAK-based flow control and error recovery influenced later protocol designs. TCP, for example, uses a sliding window mechanism with acknowledgments for both flow control and reliability.

sections.title: Problems with Current Allocation
sections.content: M. Elie from UCLA notes that the current protocol uses a complicated scheme for buffer allocation with two parallel mechanisms: control messages (CEASE, ALL, GVB, RET) and RFNM. The current RFNM is sent by the receiving IMP after the message is reconstituted and the first packet is transmitted to the host, but before the host has fully received the message. This means nothing guarantees the entire message will be accepted by the host, and the host can stop accepting data at any time. As a result, more data may arrive at the IMP from another sender before the first link is fully unblocked, causing IMP memory congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: The current system says 'message received' before actually checking that the receiving computer has the space and is ready. This causes traffic jams.

sections.title: Proposed Simplification with ACK/NAK
sections.content:
Elie proposes modifying RFNM so it is sent by the receiving host as an acknowledgment only after the message has been fully received. The host would send one of three messages:

ACK (CONTINUE): The message arrived successfully and space is available for the next message. ACK (CEASE): The message arrived successfully but no space remains for another message; stop sending. NAK (REPEAT): An error was detected; resend the message.

This single mechanism handles both flow control and error recovery. When the receiving process later processes buffered data and frees space, the host can send another ACK (CONTINUE) on that connection to resume transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets an immediate reply: 'got it, send more', 'got it, stop', or 'bad, try again'. This is much simpler than having several parallel systems.

sections.title: Benefits and Implications
sections.content:
This design has several advantages. First, it enables end-to-end error detection using checksums on the message text, since NAK (REPEAT) allows the sender to retransmit. Currently nothing ensures that bits have not been altered in transit. Second, it simplifies the buffer allocation: the receiving NCP no longer uses a complex pre-allocation scheme. Instead, allocation emerges naturally from flow control—when the receiver has space, it sends ACK (CONTINUE), and when full, it sends ACK (CEASE). The receiving process is not involved; it only sees a varying transmission rate.

Third, the scheme reduces the overhead of control messages. The IMP no longer stores messages longer than necessary waiting for deallocation. If the receiving host detects an error (checked via the NCP's checksum), the NCP can request retransmission, and the sending host repeats from buffers it has retained. This is simpler than having the IMP manage retransmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Errors can now be caught and fixed. Control is simpler. The receiving computer does not need to know all the allocation details; it just says 'yes' or 'no' to each message.
